entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Tegucigalpa, Honduras (circa 1889)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Department formed:** 1838 from predecessor
- **Administrative center:** City of Tegucigalpa, capital of Honduras; seat of Distrito Central
- **Population (Fco. Morazán dept):** ~59,000 (1881); ~60,200 (1887); ~77,700 (1901). Honduras national ~407,280 (1889).
- **Religion:** Predominantly Roman Catholic; Catedral San Miguel Arcángel was the main city parish
- **Key event:** Department renamed Francisco Morazán in 1943

## Boundary changes
- 1542–1821: Province under Captaincy General of Guatemala (New Spain)
- 1821–1838: Department under Federal Republic of Central America
- **1838–1943: 'Tegucigalpa' Department, Republic of Honduras** ← 1889 falls here
- 1943–present: Renamed Francisco Morazán

## Key record types for 1889

### Civil registration (Nacimientos)
- Collection 2135627 (Honduras, Civil Registration, 1841–1968): 12.5M records, 337,976 images, name-indexed
- Volumes directly covering 1889 for Distrito Central: Nov 1887–Jul 1889 (100% indexed), Sep 1889–Jun 1891 (100% indexed), 1888–1891 (100% indexed)

### Church baptisms
- Collection 1520634 (Honduras, Baptisms, 1730–1930): 160,997 records, name-indexed
- Collection 1823595 (Honduras, Catholic Church Records, 1633–1978): 1.8M records, name-indexed
- Main parish: Catedral San Miguel Arcángel, Distrito Central
- Also on Ancestry (col. 9889), FindMyPast, MyHeritage

### Marriage-related records
- Collection 1520638 (Honduras, Marriages, 1800–1910): 30,938 records, indexed
- Pre-nuptial investigations for Distrito Central 1889: full-text searchable only (0% name-indexed)

## Repository guide
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 2135627, 1823595, 1520634, 1520638 | Free |
| Ancestry | 9889, 9890 | Subscription |
| FindMyPast | Honduras Baptism Index 1730–1930 | Subscription |
| MyHeritage | Honduras Baptisms 1730–1930 | Subscription |

## Research tips
1. Start with civil Nacimiento search in FS 2135627 — 100% indexed volumes span 1889 for Distrito Central
2. Then search church baptisms in FS 1520634 and 1823595
3. Use 'Francisco Morazán / Distrito Central' as the place filter in FamilySearch
4. Records are in Spanish
5. FamilySearch wiki was unavailable during survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/wiki/en/Honduras_Genealogy

entry.rationale: Honduras civil registration began in 1841; FamilySearch collection 2135627 (Honduras, Civil Registration, 1841-1968) is 100% name-indexed for Nacimientos in Distrito Central with volumes directly spanning 1887-1891. A civil birth record for Guillermo filed under Micaela Salgado would be direct evidence answering the question. Search first as highest-probability, free, fully-indexed source. Use 'Francisco Morazán / Distrito Central' as the place filter (department renamed from Tegucigalpa to Francisco Morazán in 1943).

Catholic baptism registers for Tegucigalpa's main parish (Catedral San Miguel Arcángel) and the broader Honduras church record corpus are name-indexed in FS collection 1520634 (Honduras, Baptisms, 1730-1930: 160,997 records) and collection 1823595 (Honduras, Catholic Church Records, 1633-1978: 1.8M records). A baptism entry would record the child's name, baptism date, mother (Micaela Salgado), father, and godparents — direct evidence. Search a ±3-year window around 1889 to account for imprecision in the stated year.

FAN corroboration: search civil Nacimientos (collection 2135627) for the two known daughters of Micaela Salgado, born circa 1874 and 1884 in Tegucigalpa, to confirm her presence in the Distrito Central civil registration records and establish the pattern of registration. Finding the daughters' entries under Micaela Salgado validates her identity in the record set and contextualizes any absence or presence of a Guillermo entry in 1889.

Full-text co-occurrence search: if indexed searches (items 1-2) return no result, execute a full-text search across unindexed FamilySearch image volumes using the co-occurrence pattern '+Salgado +Guillermo' (and variant '+Micaela +Salgado') unscoped across the entire Honduras corpus. Per the record-type guide, for Latin-American compound surnames this surfaces acts not reachable by name-indexed search — including browse-only baptism volumes not captured in collections 1520634 or 2135627. Route this item to the search-full-text skill.

Ancestry collection 9889 (Honduras Select Baptisms, 1730-1930) mirrors the FamilySearch baptism index but applies its own indexing pipeline and may surface variant spellings or entries missed in the FS search. MyHeritage and FindMyPast carry the same index. Search Ancestry as a paid-repository fallback if FS indexed search (item 2) returns nothing.

If a Guillermo Salgado was baptized in 1889 but died in infancy or childhood, a civil death record (Defunciones, collection 2135627) or church burial record (collection 1823595) for Distrito Central would corroborate his existence and relationship to Micaela Salgado. Defunciones volumes for Tegucigalpa 1888-1891 are 100% indexed. A death record for an infant Guillermo son of Micaela Salgado is positive evidence that the baptism occurred even if the baptism record itself is not found.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary — Probable

**Question:** Did Micaela Salgado of Tegucigalpa, Honduras have a son named Guillermo, baptized in 1889?

**Conclusion:** Micaela Salgado (born 1854, Tegucigalpa; id 9XGG-PW4) probably had a son named Guillermo Salgado, baptized 20 October 1889 at San Miguel parish, Tegucigalpa, Francisco Morazán, Honduras.

### Evidence

**Direct evidence — the baptism record.** An indexed entry from the FamilySearch collection "Honduras, registros parroquiales y diocesanos, 1633-1978" records the baptism of Guillermo Salgado on 20 October 1889 at San Miguel church in Tegucigalpa. The entry names the mother as "Micaila Salgado."[^1] This record is an *original* source containing *primary* information — the officiating clergyman recorded the event contemporaneously — and constitutes *direct* evidence of both the baptism and the mother-child relationship. Source classification: original / primary / direct.

**The name variant "Micaila."** The baptism record indexes the mother's given name as "Micaila" rather than "Micaela." This is a documented OCR/handwriting-transcription artifact in Catholic parish registers from this era and region. Tree person 9XGG-PW4 carries a "Micaila Salgado" birth-name variant (N6, type BirthName) sourced directly to this record, and the surname "Salgado" is exact. No alternative candidate named Micaila or Micaela Salgado in Tegucigalpa was identified; two independent civil registration records from the same locality spell the mother's given name as "Micaela."

**Corroborating identity — civil nacimiento of Raimunda de Jesus Salgado.** A civil birth registration from "Honduras, Registro Civil, 1841-1968" names "Micaela Salgado" as mother of Raimunda de Jesus Salgado, born 1864 in Tegucigalpa.[^2] The surname and locality match tree person 9XGG-PW4. Source classification: original / primary / indirect (for Micaela's identity as a Tegucigalpa mother of record in this period).

**Corroborating identity — civil nacimiento of María Norberta Salgado.** A civil birth registration from the same collection names "Micaela Salgado" as the mother of María Norberta Salgado (born 10 December 1884), and names Elena Salgado as the maternal grandmother.[^3] Elena Salgado matches the known tree person MHZ1-4X1, recorded as Micaela's own mother (relationship R1: MHZ1-4X1 → 9XGG-PW4). The grandmother's named presence in this record provides the strongest identity corroboration, linking this Micaela unambiguously to tree person 9XGG-PW4. Source classification: original / primary / indirect (for Micaela's identity).

### Conflicts

No conflicts were identified or remain unresolved as to the identity of Guillermo's mother or the fact of his baptism. The "Micaila"/"Micaela" discrepancy is an indexing variant adequately explained by period transcription practices; the surname matches exactly across all records.

### Tier: Probable

The conclusion rests on a single original source with primary direct evidence (the Catholic baptism record, src_001). The original register image was not read during this research, so the indexed transcription could not be verified against the handwritten original. Two civil registration records corroborate the mother's identity but concern different children and different informants. Because the conclusion depends on one direct source without image verification, the weight of evidence supports **probable** rather than **proved**.

A **proved** conclusion would require at minimum: (1) independent direct evidence from a second source naming Guillermo as Micaela's son — for example, a civil birth registration for Guillermo — or (2) a verified reading of the original register image confirming the indexed entry is consistent with the handwritten record.

[^1]: "Honduras, registros parroquiales y diocesanos, 1633-1978", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KXP9-FP6 : accessed 31 July 2026), entry for Guillermo Salgado and Micaila Salgado, 20 Oct 1889.
[^2]: "Honduras, Registro Civil, 1841-1968," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:Q2RY-JWDL : accessed 31 July 2026), entry for Raimunda de Jesus Salgado and Micaela Salgado.
[^3]: "Honduras, Registro Civil, 1841-1968", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XQ84-G9ZT : accessed 31 July 2026), entry for Maria Norberta Salgado, birth registration 16 December 1884, Tegucigalpa, Distrito Central, Francisco Morazán, Honduras.

verdict.narrative_for_user:
# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
You earned the **probable** tier honestly rather than reaching for **proved** — the narrative is explicit that the register image (ark:/61903/3:1:939K-R9HG-B) was never read and no second direct source names Guillermo, and it says so in plain language (Standards 43, 64-67). That's exactly the discipline this system is designed to teach. I also like that you didn't lean on the baptism record alone: pulling src_002 and src_003 to show Micaela Salgado repeatedly appearing as a Tegucigalpa mother across 1864-1891 is a legitimate way to strengthen an identity call with pattern evidence even when neither record mentions Guillermo directly.

## What to address before moving on
The whole proof hinges on one identity call: that 'Micaila' in the baptism record is the same woman as 'Micaela Salgado' (9XGG-PW4), and the narrative flatly states 'no alternative candidate ... was identified.' That's an elimination claim, and elimination claims need a home in `hypotheses[]` or `conflicts[]` — right now both arrays are empty. It's not that the reasoning is wrong; it's that it lives only in prose (a_005's `informant_bias_notes`, pe_006's rationale) with nothing a future reviewer can cite by id.

There's a second, more concrete instance of the same gap. Your own `person_evidence` (pe_008) and the exhaustive declaration already flagged that the civil-birth persona for 'Raimunda de Jesus Salgado' (I2, b. 1864, used as corroborating evidence a_007-a_012) is ten years off from the tree's existing Raimunda (9XGG-PWW, b. 1874) — and you explicitly recommended conflict-resolution for it, then set it aside as a 'side matter.' That's a defensible call, but it never made it into `conflicts[]`, and it never made it into the proof narrative either. Anyone reading `narrative_markdown` on its own has no idea this discrepancy exists in a source the proof cites as identity corroboration. That's a Standard 43 transparency problem as much as a structural one.

## Worth considering
log_003 turned up a third spelling, 'Micada Salgado' (result X7X3-FXH3), while you were searching for Elena Salgado — and it was never opened or ruled out. It's probably nothing, but the proof's 'no alternative candidate identified' line is only as strong as the leads you actually chased down. Worth a quick read-and-log, or an explicit note on why it was set aside.

## What would change my mind
Add a `hypotheses` entry for the Micaila/Micaela candidate elimination (what you searched, why nothing else surfaced) and a `conflicts` entry for the Raimunda 1864-vs-1874 discrepancy with a proper resolution_rationale — both cited by id from the proof or its supporting assertions. That converts reasoning that currently only exists in your head (and in scattered `informant_bias_notes`) into an auditable record, which is what turns 'I thought about this' into 'I can show you I thought about this.' None of this moves the tier — probable still looks like the right call to me — but it closes the audit trail gap a peer reviewer would flag first.
